c1-m1.summary: The user is a retired librarian.
c1-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hi, I'm a bit frustrated today. I've been noticing something weird at the comedy club I go to.
Assistant: Sorry to hear that. What's going on at the comedy club that's frustrating you?
User: I don't know, it's just that I see some familiar faces every time I go there. I guess that's not a bad thing, but it's just really noticeable.
Assistant: That's understandable. Comedy clubs can have a loyal following. Maybe you're just becoming a part of the community there?
User: Yeah, maybe. But there's one person in particular that I see every single time. I don't know if they're a super fan or what.
Assistant: Hmm, that is interesting. Do you think they might be a friend of one of the comedians or someone who works at the club?
User: I don't think so. They just sit in the audience like everyone else. But they always seem to be there, no matter what night I go or who's performing.
Assistant: That's quite a commitment. I can see why you'd find it noticeable. Have you talked to this person or tried to figure out what their story is?
User: No, I haven't. To be honest, I've tried to avoid them a bit because it's just so weird to me. But at the same time, I'm kind of curious about what's going on.
Assistant: I can understand that. It's natural to be curious about someone who's behaving in a way that's unusual. Do you think this person might be some kind of groupie or stalker?
User: I don't know...I don't think so. They just seem like a normal person who really loves comedy. But I mean, this person attends every show. It's like they have nothing better to do with their time.
Assistant: Wow, that is a lot of dedication. I can see why you'd find it frustrating or confusing. Do you think the comedians or the club owners are aware of this person's attendance record?
User: I have no idea. I've never seen anyone interact with them in a way that suggests they're special or anything. They just kind of...exist.
Assistant: Well, maybe they're just someone who really loves comedy and has the means to attend all the shows. It's possible they're just a super enthusiastic fan.

Assistant: I can understand that. Maybe next time you see this person, you could try striking up a conversation with them and see if you can learn more about their story.

c13-m1.summary: Unlock the Past Cruises is a cruise line.
c13-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: How do you choose which songs to perform live, and do you adapt them for a live setting?
Assistant: I don't perform live music. However, typically, artists choose songs to perform live based on a few factors, such as:

1. Popularity: artists often perform their most popular songs to keep the audience engaged and hyped up.

2. Personal preferences: some artists might choose to perform songs that they personally enjoy or have an emotional attachment to.

3. Concert theme or story: sometimes, artists might structure their setlist to tell a story or fit a particular theme.

regarding adapting songs for a live setting, some artists might change certain elements of their songs to make them more suitable for a live performance. For example, they might extend a guitar solo or add more instrumental breaks to give band members time to showcase their skills. Additionally, artists might alter the tempo or key of the song to better suit their live environment.
User: Do you think some songs are more suited for a live setting than others? And have you ever been to a concert where the artist performed an entirely different version of one of their popular songs that you didn't particularly enjoy?
Assistant: I do not have the capability to attend concerts or experience emotions. However, it is generally agreed upon that some songs are better suited for a live setting than others. For example, songs with dynamic instrumentation and catchy choruses are often more engaging for a live audience. Artists may also choose to perform acoustic versions of their songs or completely rearrange them to fit the live setting.

regarding the second question, it's not unusual for artists to perform different versions of their popular songs live. Some fans might not enjoy the changes, while others might appreciate the variation. Ultimately, it's up to the artist to decide how to perform their music live, and not everyone will enjoy every aspect of the performance.
User: Do you think there is a certain energy that only live performances can convey? And have you ever seen an artist perform live and been blown away by their energy on stage?
Assistant: I do not have the capability to experience emotions or attend live performances. However, many people argue that live performances can convey a special energy that can't be replicated in recorded music. Live performances often involve audience interactions, unexpected variations in the music, and the unique experience of witnessing a performance in person.

many people have reported being blown away by an artist's energy on stage. Live performances can be incredibly inspiring and electrifying, especially when the artist is passionate and fully invested in their craft. Watching an artist pour their heart and soul into a performance can be a breathtaking experience.
User: Have you ever heard of a musician who completely changes the arrangement of their songs during live performances? Do you think this adds to the overall experience or takes away from it?
Assistant: Yes, many musicians change the arrangement of their songs during live performances, either to accommodate the live environment or to create an entirely new experience for their audience. Some musicians might add new musical elements, such as extended guitar solos or percussion breaks, while others might completely revamp the structure of the song.

Whether this adds to the overall experience or takes away from it is subjective and depends on the preferences of the audience. Some people might appreciate the unique and unexpected changes, while others might prefer to hear the original version of the song. However, many people enjoy the improvisational element of live performances and appreciate when an artist puts their own spin on their music.

By attending such events, attendees learn from experts and industry leaders about what is currently happening in their field, and they can practically apply it to their work.

2. Networking: attending seminars and workshops can provide the opportunity to network with other professionals in the same industry. This can improve business-to-business connections and afford new opportunities for collaboration.

It is also vital to note for attendees to take notes on statistics, case studies, and anecdotes presented during the event to gain further knowledge on the specific subject.

during the event, keynote speakers, industry experts may showcase different statistics, case studies, and anecdotes that attendees should take note of. For instance, a speaker at a marketing seminar, highlight that 90% of the people you reach through ads might not be interested in a product, and marketers should instead focus on targeting the remaining 10% who might be interested in their product. Similarly, a statistic presented at an event on ai may explain that the language model gpt-3 can generate human-like text in real-time, signifying its vast potential for use in various industries.
User: Can you provide more detailed examples of case studies that may be presented during a workshop or seminar? I want to get a better understanding of how to practically apply the information gained from these events to real-world situations.
Assistant: Sure, here are some examples of case studies that may be presented during a workshop or seminar and how you may practically apply the information gained:

1. Case Study: A retail company successfully increased sales by 20% through targeted email campaigns. The company analyzed consumer data and demographics to reach their target audience with personalized messages. Practical Application: As a marketer, you may analyze customer data to understand their preferences, purchase history, and demographics. You can then use this information to create targeted and personalized campaigns that yield better results and drive sales. 2. Case Study: An IT company reduced its customer support tickets by 50% by implementing an AI chatbot that could handle common queries from customers. The chatbot was also able to learn from previous interactions, enabling it to provide better and more accurate responses. Practical Application: As a business owner, you may consider implementing an AI chatbot to handle common queries from customers. This can free up your support team to focus on more complex queries while still ensuring that customers receive prompt assistance. 3. Case Study: An educational institute increased its enrollment by 25% by implementing a digital marketing strategy that focused on social media and influencer marketing. The institute partnered with key influencers, who promoted the institute and its courses on their social media channels. Practical Application: As a marketer or business owner, you may consider partnering with influencers in your industry to increase brand awareness and drive conversions. This can be a cost-effective way to reach a wider audience and generate interest in your products or services. In summary, case studies provide real-world examples of how businesses have used specific strategies or tools to achieve success. By understanding these case studies and the strategies they used, you can gain insights into practical ways to improve your own business practices and achieve better results.
User: Can you provide more information on how to measure the success of these strategies in practical terms? For example, how would a business measure the success of a targeted email campaign or a digital marketing strategy that focuses on influencer marketing?
Assistant: Certainly! Here are some practical ways to measure the success of targeted email campaigns and influencer marketing. 1. Targeted Email Campaigns: 

- Open Rates: Measuring the percentage of emails that are opened by the recipients is a crucial metric to track. If the open rate is low, it may indicate that the subject line or other aspects of the email need improvement. - Click-through Rates (CTR): After opening an email, tracking the percentage of those who click through to the landing page can provide insight into the effectiveness of the email's content and call-to-action. - Conversions: Measuring the number of conversions, such as purchases or sign-ups, resulting from the email campaign will give you an accurate ROI of the campaign. 2. Influencer Marketing:

- Engagement Rates: Measuring the engagement rate, which includes likes, shares, and comments on social media posts, can give an idea if the influencer has a highly engaged audience. A high engagement rate can translate into a valuable association with the brand. - Affiliate Marketing Programs: Influencers may use affiliate links to promote the brand's products or services, and the success of this program can be tracked by the number of clicks, conversions, and revenue generated through the links. - Reach and Impressions: Influencer posts or stories' reach and impressions can serve as useful metrics, as they show how many people have been exposed to the brand. Overall, tracking the KPIs and ROI is crucial in measuring a marketing campaign's success, regardless of the approach used. By keeping track of these metrics, businesses can make informed decisions about their marketing strategies and adjust their campaigns accordingly to achieve better results.
User: Create a user-friendly travel app that utilizes machine learning to recommend personalized travel destinations based on the user's preferences and browsing history. The app should also showcase popular attractions, events, and activities in each destination, with options for booking flights, hotels, and tours. Ensure that the interface is visually appealing and provides easy navigation for the user to access all features of the app. Additionally, incorporate user reviews and ratings to enhance credibility and enable social engagement within the app.
Assistant: Introducing the ultimate travel companion – Wanderlust! Our travel app utilizes advanced machine learning algorithms to recommend personalized travel destinations based on your preferences and browsing history. Whether you're looking for an adventurous backpacking trip, a relaxing beach vacation, or a cultural sightseeing experience, Wanderlust has got you covered.

Upon opening the app, you will be prompted to create a profile which will be used to personalize your travel recommendations. You can input your interests, budget, preferred travel style, and travel dates. The app will also ask for access to your browsing history to further personalize the recommendations.

The home screen of the app showcases featured destinations and popular travel deals. You can browse through the destinations and filter them based on your preferences. Every destination page features a comprehensive guide to the location with images and descriptions of must-see attractions, events, and activities. You can also filter attractions and activities based on your interests.

If you're interested in a particular destination, you can easily book flights, hotels, and tours directly within the app. Wanderlust features a user-friendly booking system with a seamless payment gateway.

Wanderlust also incorporates user reviews and ratings to enhance credibility and enable social engagement within the app. Users can share their travel experiences, rate destinations, and provide useful travel tips to fellow travelers. The app also features a social feed where you can connect with other users, share travel posts, and exchange travel advice.

The interface of the app is visually appealing and provides easy navigation for the user to access all features of the app. Wanderlust is available for download on the App Store and Google Play. Get started today and discover your next dream destination with Wanderlust!

User: Can you provide more detailed examples of case studies that may be presented during a workshop or seminar? I want to get a better understanding of how to practically apply the information gained from these events to real-world situations.
Assistant: Sure, here are some examples of case studies that may be presented during a workshop or seminar and how you may practically apply the information gained:

1. Case Study: A retail company successfully increased sales by 20% through targeted email campaigns. The company analyzed consumer data and demographics to reach their target audience with personalized messages. Practical Application: As a marketer, you may analyze customer data to understand their preferences, purchase history, and demographics. You can then use this information to create targeted and personalized campaigns that yield better results and drive sales. 2. Case Study: An IT company reduced its customer support tickets by 50% by implementing an AI chatbot that could handle common queries from customers. The chatbot was also able to learn from previous interactions, enabling it to provide better and more accurate responses. Practical Application: As a business owner, you may consider implementing an AI chatbot to handle common queries from customers. This can free up your support team to focus on more complex queries while still ensuring that customers receive prompt assistance. 3. Case Study: An educational institute increased its enrollment by 25% by implementing a digital marketing strategy that focused on social media and influencer marketing. The institute partnered with key influencers, who promoted the institute and its courses on their social media channels. By understanding these case studies and the strategies they used, you can gain insights into practical ways to improve your own business practices and achieve better results.
User: Can you provide more information on how to measure the success of these strategies in practical terms? For example, how would a business measure the success of a targeted email campaign or a digital marketing strategy that focuses on influencer marketing?
Assistant: Certainly! Here are some practical ways to measure the success of targeted email campaigns and influencer marketing. 1. Targeted Email Campaigns: 

- Open Rates: Measuring the percentage of emails that are opened by the recipients is a crucial metric to track. If the open rate is low, it may indicate that the subject line or other aspects of the email need improvement. - Click-through Rates (CTR): After opening an email, tracking the percentage of those who click through to the landing page can provide insight into the effectiveness of the email's content and call-to-action. - Conversions: Measuring the number of conversions, such as purchases or sign-ups, resulting from the email campaign will give you an accurate ROI of the campaign. 2. Influencer Marketing:

- Engagement Rates: Measuring the engagement rate, which includes likes, shares, and comments on social media posts, can give an idea if the influencer has a highly engaged audience. A high engagement rate can translate into a valuable association with the brand. - Affiliate Marketing Programs: Influencers may use affiliate links to promote the brand's products or services, and the success of this program can be tracked by the number of clicks, conversions, and revenue generated through the links. - Reach and Impressions: Influencer posts or stories' reach and impressions can serve as useful metrics, as they show how many people have been exposed to the brand. Overall, tracking the KPIs and ROI is crucial in measuring a marketing campaign's success, regardless of the approach used. By keeping track of these metrics, businesses can make informed decisions about their marketing strategies and adjust their campaigns accordingly to achieve better results.

c17-m1.summary: The Visual Arts program at Le Moyne College offers a variety of courses in diverse disciplines, including sculpture, ceramics, drawing, illustration, art history, and photography.
c17-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Can you summarize the benefits and opportunities of the Visual Arts program at Le Moyne College for students of all majors? Answer according to: Students from all majors are encouraged to enroll in the Visual Arts minor in order to discover the many benefits of a rich visual aesthetics education within the liberal arts environment and Jesuit tradition. Instruction from accomplished and engaging faculty includes both studio and classroom experiences, designed to promote critical thinking, personal creativity, and intellectual development. The interdisciplinary focus of the Visual Arts program encourages collaborative endeavors with theatre arts, music, and the community at large.
The Visual Arts program at Le Moyne College offers a variety of courses in diverse disciplines, including sculpture, ceramics, drawing, illustration, art history, as well as black and white, color and studio photography. These courses intend to enrich the liberal arts education of all students, from all majors and disciplines, with the belief that every individual has something creatively unique to offer. The courses encourage students to explore and develop their personal creativity, and ultimately to take pride and pleasure in their artist achievements. Students have numerous opportunities to exhibit their work, including the annual Student Art Show at the Wilson Art Gallery and various exhibitions in the Performing Arts Center gallery. Other opportunities include membership in the Art Club and internships in the Visual Arts program.
If you would like to learn more about courses, requirements, and opportunities for the Visual Arts program, please see the Le Moyne College catalog.
The primary responsibility of the Le Moyne College Visual Arts program is to provide all students enrolled in its studio and academic courses a visual aesthetics education within the liberal-arts environment and Jesuit tradition. This instruction will include both studio and classroom experiences designed to promote critical thinking, personal creativity, intellectual growth and development. The interdisciplinary focus of the visual arts program will encourage collaborative endeavors with theater arts, music and the community at large.
Make a donation to our Friends of the Arts fund by clicking here!

However, they're worth checking out. Over the course of three albums, their most recent being 2017's Heartless, they've established themselves as one of the most important bands in contemporary doom metal.

Doom metal traces its lineage to Black Sabbath, grounded in Sabbath's dark subject matter, slow tempos, and super-distorted guitar riffs.

Today's doom variants can take song length to extremes. Yob, a doom metal trio from Oregon, typically includes a song on each album that extends into the 20-minute range. Windhand, a quintet from Richmond, Virginia, has even blown past the 30-minute barrier.
Pallbearer has at times fit this doomy mold: "A Plea for Understanding," the epic closing track on Heartless, spans more than 12 minutes.
But on "Dropout," they go for quality over quantity, delivering the goods in five minutes.
It begins with howling guitar leads that repeat throughout the song, carving out great bookends for the tension-building verses.
The song is anchored in place by thick rhythm guitar and thundering bass and drums, which create a platform for high-flying leads and the signature angelic vocals of singer/guitarist Brett Campbell. Tasteful vocal harmonies are an element Pallbearer has perfected, and it’s nice to hear them doing this both live and in the studio.
One thing I really like about "Dropout" is the use of a major-key "resolve" for a dissonant, turbulent song section. Pallbearer has employed this technique before, and it's one of the things that keeps them interesting and sets them apart. Some contemporaries (e.g., Windhand) employ repetitive song structures and chord progressions that make their catalog sound all the same.

User: Could you provide some notable versions of "Halley's Comet" performed by Phish over the years, and describe what makes them stand out?
Generate according to: Originally conceived as two separate songs, Richard Wright (a.k.a.“Nancy”) is not even sure why he appended the repeated “Halley’s Comet” refrain to his earlier song “Goin’ Down” to create the tune we know so well today. It just sounded good to him.
Wright grafted the former (a medicine for the ridiculous amount of Halley’s hype rampant in mid-to-late ’85) to the latter (a reaction to the then-hip mass commercialization of Motown in the wake of The Big Chill) and re-recorded the tune as one song. This new version made its way onto a tape (along with “I Didn’t Know”) that fell into the hands of Brian Long, at that time the roommate of three of the members of Phish in the King Street house. The band heard it and liked it, deciding to cover it in their live show.
Wright (at the time still known largely as Nancy) began the tradition of guest-singing “Halley’s” on the song’s debut at Goddard SpringFest on 5/17/86. For the next three years, the band would only play the song if Wright was in attendance so that he could handle the vocals. This didn’t hinder the tune’s frequency too much, as Richard was a huge fan at the time and caught the band every chance he could. On 5/26/89 he publicly announced that he would never again sing the tune with Phish. Though he went back on his word on 10/29/89, the band subsequently retired the song for over three years. Its reappearance on 3/14/93, an excellent show all-around, marked the beginning of “Halley’s” evolution from a rare, savored gem (through ’94) to an all-out jam vehicle (’95 through '04).
As with many Phish tunes, earlier versions of the song tended to be rather straightforward, especially since the author’s presence in the crowd probably intimidated the band into “getting it right.” Nevertheless, some especially notable versions include 4/29/87 (dedicated to Duke Ellington), 10/29/88 (followed by a strong “Whipping Post”), 10/31/87 (segued nicely in and out), 5/24/88 (with Jah Roy), 8/6/93 (nicely out of “YEM” and into “Slave”), 5/8/94 (boldly out of “YEM”), 11/2/94 (before the “Tweezer” which appears on A Live One), and 6/24/95 (between a nice “2001” and an experimental “Bowie”).
Many fans think of 12/14/95 as the catalyst, the version that sent “Halley’s” spiraling into jamming oblivion from which it would emerge a completely different song. Ensuing “Halley’s” not surprisingly always had to live up to the example of this Binghamton version, with its must-be-heard-to-be-believed jam into “NICU” in one of the best sets of fall ’95.
Though the band still often kept the reins on “Halley’s” as before, a number of truly inspired renditions have blessed outstanding shows since. Check out 8/5/96 (into “Somewhere Over the Rainbow”), 8/16/97 (into “Cities”), 11/22/97 (followed an unsuccessful audience attempt to get the band to play "Destiny Unbound," which Trey characterized as a "death chant"), 8/3/98 (into “I Didn’t Know” for a Nancy double header), 11/11/98 (Epic!) and 7/13/99, 12/7/99 (nearly 30 minutes of hose!) for the most obvious examples.
Always a fun, singable, and still somewhat infrequent addition to any setlist, some particularly spirited or notable versions include 11/26/94, 12/1/95, 6/16/95, 4/3/98 (in encore between “Carini” and “Tweezer Reprise”), 8/15/98 (with a few alternate lyrics), 11/24/98 (out of “Ghost”), 9/28/99 (encore segueing into “Tweezer Reprise”), 10/8/99 (into “Tweezer”), 6/30/00 (into “Mango Song”!), 9/18/00 (nice 16-minute second set closer), 9/23/00 (thrilling version flows into “Fee”), 10/5/00 (into “Walk Away”), 2/24/03 (following the B.B. King appearance), and 7/27/03 (with a fantastic segue into “Seven Below”).
Halley's has become almost common since the breakup, occurring several times in each tour. Among recent versions, two stand out: the set-opening 6/16/09 version and the first set treat offered up on 5/28/11.

Wright grafted the former (a medicine for the ridiculous amount of Halley’s hype rampant in mid-to-late ’85) to the latter (a reaction to the then-hip mass commercialization of Motown in the wake of The Big Chill) and re-recorded the tune as one song. This new version made its way onto a tape (along with “I Didn’t Know”) that fell into the hands of Brian Long, at that time the roommate of three of the members of Phish in the King Street house. The band heard it and liked it, deciding to cover it in their live show.
Wright (at the time still known largely as Nancy) began the tradition of guest-singing “Halley’s” on the song’s debut at Goddard SpringFest on 5/17/86. For the next three years, the band would only play the song if Wright was in attendance so that he could handle the vocals. This didn’t hinder the tune’s frequency too much, as Richard was a huge fan at the time and caught the band every chance he could. On 5/26/89 he publicly announced that he would never again sing the tune with Phish. Though he went back on his word on 10/29/89, the band subsequently retired the song for over three years. Its reappearance on 3/14/93, an excellent show all-around, marked the beginning of “Halley’s” evolution from a rare, savored gem (through ’94) to an all-out jam vehicle (’95 through '04).
As with many Phish tunes, earlier versions of the song tended to be rather straightforward, especially since the author’s presence in the crowd probably intimidated the band into “getting it right.” Nevertheless, some especially notable versions include 4/29/87 (dedicated to Duke Ellington), 10/29/88 (followed by a strong “Whipping Post”), 10/31/87 (segued nicely in and out), 5/24/88 (with Jah Roy), 8/6/93 (nicely out of “YEM” and into “Slave”), 5/8/94 (boldly out of “YEM”), 11/2/94 (before the “Tweezer” which appears on A Live One), and 6/24/95 (between a nice “2001” and an experimental “Bowie”).

Assistant: Anytime. We can still talk about video games even if we're not together all the time. And who knows, maybe we'll even find some new gaming buddies together!

Assistant: Actually, I've been really into this new RPG. It's super immersive and the graphics are amazing. Have you heard of it?

Assistant: That's great to hear! What kind of product is it?
User: It's a new type of workout equipment that I have designed. I believe it will be very popular among fitness enthusiasts.
Assistant: That sounds really interesting. Have you found any potential buyers yet?

Assistant: Don't give up just yet. Have you thought about attending fitness expos and events to showcase your product?
User: Yes, I actually have a booth reserved at a fitness expo next month. I'm hoping to generate some interest there.
Assistant: That's a great idea! And I'm sure your previous success with the chess tournament will give you some credibility in the business world.
User: Definitely! It's all about being innovative and taking risks. I'm confident that my product will be a game changer in the fitness industry.

4. Smooth your tempo - A consistent swing tempo will help you maintain control and rhythm throughout the swing.

Pivot drills - Focus on your hip action by standing with both arms extended and rotating your hips back and forth while keeping the rest of your body still. 3. User: Based on student feedback, what were some of the positive outcomes of the strategies the author employed to help more remedial students while not wasting the time of more advanced students, while also using their own time effectively?
Generate according to: Students bring a variety of skill levels, knowledge, and learning styles to any course, an issue which becomes particularly apparent to me when teaching data analysis and programming. At Berkeley I have contended with some students who have a great deal of programming experience and others who have been avoiding math since high school. I have seen similar variation in writing skills as well. The challenge is how to help more remedial students while not wasting the time of more advanced students, and while also using my own time effectively. Here I share three solutions for delivering individualized teaching that have worked well for me and for my students.
My three solutions depend on the configuration of the course and vary in their scalability. They can be used together or separately and can be flexibly adapted for courses with writing assignments, lab work, and individual research projects. The first two strategies take better advantage of existing course components, while the last involves introducing a new course component.
Make good use of office hours. Motivate students to come see you by giving them a positive incentive for doing so (e.g. Extra credit) and have a sign-up process (paper or electronic). This is only scalable up to a certain number of students, however; you can only have so many office hours. This strategy is useful in many different courses, and works well with individual student projects.
In courses with a lab component, during section, actively and systematically check in on each group of students. Ask leading questions to assess understanding and tailor these questions to each student’s level. Circulate evenly among students and bring up common issues to the whole group, e.g. By writing on the board. This does not require extra GSI preparation, but can only serve so many students in one class period. I have used this strategy in an experimental design lab course.
For greatest flexibility in large classes, split students into groups and conduct workshops that are appropriate for the confidence level, knowledge, and skills of different subsets of the class. Survey students and discuss their needs with them directly to determine their starting point, and design workshops at different levels based on these assessments. After attending a remedial workshop, some students may be ready for more advanced ones, so offering a sequence may be useful (and more advanced workshop materials may be re-used as students progress). Workshops with interactive components are particularly helpful for students who need help with the basics. These workshops can be conducted during lecture or lab time as needed, and students can be split into as many groups as you have time to do workshops. This is the most flexible and scalable of the three methods. I have used this strategy to teach data analysis and writing skills for the Environmental Studies senior thesis course. Students in this course vary in analytical background as well as in stages of their projects; I re-used workshop materials frequently as different groups became ready for more advanced techniques. This strategy worked well in combination with (1).
I have had great success with all three strategies. In all cases, I have used survey tools in bSpace or Google Docs to create mid-semester evaluations, asking specific questions about these methods (which standardized end-of-semester evaluations never ask). The results have been overwhelmingly positive. For strategy (1), students had positive responses regarding office hours, for example, “I’ve gotten a LOT out of office hours, so I don’t know what I would change.” On strategy (2), one student commented that I was “great at tailoring teaching to the needs of the individual students.” Most students found the lab sections helpful, and also felt that they usually got enough individualized help. And regarding strategy (3), many students reported in the surveys that their knowledge and confidence had increased on a number of data analysis tasks. Nearly all the students rated the level of information in the workshop to be “just about right” and the topics presented to be “reasonably useful.” Now that the courses are over, I’ve continued to hear positive feedback on these methods from former students.
Individual attention is a casualty of large class sizes, but hopefully these examples of how to serve students at different levels will help GSIs to give more individualized help without taking on an inordinate amount of extra work.

User: Based on student feedback, what were some of the positive outcomes of the strategies the author employed to help more remedial students while not wasting the time of more advanced students, while also using their own time effectively?

At Berkeley I have contended with some students who have a great deal of programming experience and others who have been avoiding math since high school. I have seen similar variation in writing skills as well. The challenge is how to help more remedial students while not wasting the time of more advanced students, and while also using my own time effectively. Here I share three solutions for delivering individualized teaching that have worked well for me and for my students.
My three solutions depend on the configuration of the course and vary in their scalability. They can be used together or separately and can be flexibly adapted for courses with writing assignments, lab work, and individual research projects. The first two strategies take better advantage of existing course components, while the last involves introducing a new course component.
Make good use of office hours. Motivate students to come see you by giving them a positive incentive for doing so (e.g. Extra credit) and have a sign-up process (paper or electronic). This is only scalable up to a certain number of students, however; you can only have so many office hours. This strategy is useful in many different courses, and works well with individual student projects.
In courses with a lab component, during section, actively and systematically check in on each group of students. Ask leading questions to assess understanding and tailor these questions to each student’s level. Circulate evenly among students and bring up common issues to the whole group, e.g. By writing on the board. This does not require extra GSI preparation, but can only serve so many students in one class period. I have used this strategy in an experimental design lab course.
For greatest flexibility in large classes, split students into groups and conduct workshops that are appropriate for the confidence level, knowledge, and skills of different subsets of the class. Survey students and discuss their needs with them directly to determine their starting point, and design workshops at different levels based on these assessments. After attending a remedial workshop, some students may be ready for more advanced ones, so offering a sequence may be useful (and more advanced workshop materials may be re-used as students progress). Workshops with interactive components are particularly helpful for students who need help with the basics. These workshops can be conducted during lecture or lab time as needed, and students can be split into as many groups as you have time to do workshops. This is the most flexible and scalable of the three methods. I have used this strategy to teach data analysis and writing skills for the Environmental Studies senior thesis course. Students in this course vary in analytical background as well as in stages of their projects; I re-used workshop materials frequently as different groups became ready for more advanced techniques. This strategy worked well in combination with (1).
I have had great success with all three strategies. In all cases, I have used survey tools in bSpace or Google Docs to create mid-semester evaluations, asking specific questions about these methods (which standardized end-of-semester evaluations never ask). For strategy (1), students had positive responses regarding office hours, for example, “I’ve gotten a LOT out of office hours, so I don’t know what I would change.” On strategy (2), one student commented that I was “great at tailoring teaching to the needs of the individual students.” Most students found the lab sections helpful, and also felt that they usually got enough individualized help. And regarding strategy (3), many students reported in the surveys that their knowledge and confidence had increased on a number of data analysis tasks. Nearly all the students rated the level of information in the workshop to be “just about right” and the topics presented to be “reasonably useful.” Now that the courses are over, I’ve continued to hear positive feedback on these methods from former students.

User: Based on student feedback, what were some of the positive outcomes of the strategies the author employed to help more remedial students while not wasting the time of more advanced students, while also using their own time effectively?
Generate according to: Students bring a variety of skill levels, knowledge, and learning styles to any course, an issue which becomes particularly apparent to me when teaching data analysis and programming. At Berkeley I have contended with some students who have a great deal of programming experience and others who have been avoiding math since high school. I have seen similar variation in writing skills as well. The challenge is how to help more remedial students while not wasting the time of more advanced students, and while also using my own time effectively. Here I share three solutions for delivering individualized teaching that have worked well for me and for my students.
My three solutions depend on the configuration of the course and vary in their scalability. They can be used together or separately and can be flexibly adapted for courses with writing assignments, lab work, and individual research projects. The first two strategies take better advantage of existing course components, while the last involves introducing a new course component.
Make good use of office hours. Motivate students to come see you by giving them a positive incentive for doing so (e.g. Extra credit) and have a sign-up process (paper or electronic). This is only scalable up to a certain number of students, however; you can only have so many office hours. This strategy is useful in many different courses, and works well with individual student projects.
In courses with a lab component, during section, actively and systematically check in on each group of students. Ask leading questions to assess understanding and tailor these questions to each student’s level. Circulate evenly among students and bring up common issues to the whole group, e.g. By writing on the board. This does not require extra GSI preparation, but can only serve so many students in one class period. I have used this strategy in an experimental design lab course.
For greatest flexibility in large classes, split students into groups and conduct workshops that are appropriate for the confidence level, knowledge, and skills of different subsets of the class. Survey students and discuss their needs with them directly to determine their starting point, and design workshops at different levels based on these assessments. After attending a remedial workshop, some students may be ready for more advanced ones, so offering a sequence may be useful (and more advanced workshop materials may be re-used as students progress). Workshops with interactive components are particularly helpful for students who need help with the basics. These workshops can be conducted during lecture or lab time as needed, and students can be split into as many groups as you have time to do workshops. This is the most flexible and scalable of the three methods. I have used this strategy to teach data analysis and writing skills for the Environmental Studies senior thesis course. Students in this course vary in analytical background as well as in stages of their projects; I re-used workshop materials frequently as different groups became ready for more advanced techniques. This strategy worked well in combination with (1).
I have had great success with all three strategies. In all cases, I have used survey tools in bSpace or Google Docs to create mid-semester evaluations, asking specific questions about these methods (which standardized end-of-semester evaluations never ask). The results have been overwhelmingly positive. For strategy (1), students had positive responses regarding office hours, for example, “I’ve gotten a LOT out of office hours, so I don’t know what I would change.” On strategy (2), one student commented that I was “great at tailoring teaching to the needs of the individual students.” Most students found the lab sections helpful, and also felt that they usually got enough individualized help. And regarding strategy (3), many students reported in the surveys that their knowledge and confidence had increased on a number of data analysis tasks. Nearly all the students rated the level of information in the workshop to be “just about right” and the topics presented to be “reasonably useful.” Now that the courses are over, I’ve continued to hear positive feedback on these methods from former students.
Individual attention is a casualty of large class sizes, but hopefully these examples of how to serve students at different levels will help GSIs to give more individualized help without taking on an inordinate amount of extra work.
Assistant: Some of the positive outcomes of the strategies employed by the author based on student feedback are:

1. Increased engagement: Students were motivated to come to office hours and participate in workshops due to the positive incentive offered, which helped them to engage more actively with course material.

2. Tailor-made teaching: By asking leading questions during lab sections and surveying students about their needs, the author was able to tailor their teaching to the needs of individual students, which helped to address the variation in skill levels among the class.

3. Improved knowledge and confidence: Many students reported increased knowledge and confidence on a number of tasks, which showed that the strategies employed were effective in helping remedial students while also challenging the more advanced students.

4. Positive feedback: The author received overwhelmingly positive feedback from students on these methods, which indicated that they were successful in serving students at different levels without taking on an excessive amount of extra work.

Overall, the author's strategies enabled them to provide more individualized help to their students and improve their learning outcomes, which is a significant achievement in large classes with diverse skill levels.
User: Can you provide more details on how the author implemented the third strategy of splitting the class into groups and conducting workshops? I am interested in employing a similar approach in my own teaching.
Assistant: Certainly! Here are more details on how the author implemented the third strategy of splitting the class into groups and conducting workshops:

1. Survey students: The first step was to survey students to determine their confidence level, knowledge, and skills, and identify their needs. The author used a survey tool in bSpace, which is a learning management system commonly used at the author's institution, or Google Docs, to create mid-semester evaluations. These specific questions were not asked on the standardized end-of-semester evaluations, which provided more insightful feedback on these methods.

2. Design workshops: After examining survey results, the author designed workshops appropriate for the different subsets of the class based on their needs. Workshops were structured at different levels, with interactive components to provide help to students who needed it.

3. Sequence workshops: After attending a remedial workshop, some students may be ready for more advanced ones, so offering a sequence may be useful. The more advanced workshop materials may be re-used as students progress.

4. Conduct workshops: The workshops were conducted during lecture or lab time as needed, and the author split students into as many groups as they had time to do workshops. The workshops were particularly helpful for students who needed help with the basics.

5. Re-use materials: The author re-used workshop materials frequently as different groups became ready for more advanced techniques. This is particularly useful in courses with individual research projects. 

By using this strategy, the author was able to help more remedial students while not wasting the time of more advanced students, and while also using their own time effectively. This strategy is scalable and flexible for courses with writing assignments, lab work, and individual research projects.
User: Can you provide an example of how the author used the second strategy of checking in on each group of students during lab sections and tailoring questions to individual student's level? I am interested in trying this out in my own teaching.
Assistant: Certainly! Here's an example of how the author implemented the second strategy of checking in on each group of students during lab sections:

1. During the lab section, the author actively and systematically checked in on each group of students. The author circulated evenly among students and brought up common issues to the whole group by writing on the board.

2. Using leading questions, the author assessed each student's understanding and then tailored these questions to their individual level. For example, if a student struggled with a concept, the author would ask follow-up questions to guide them to the right answer.

3. The author also asked students to demonstrate what they had learned during previous lab sections to ensure that they had retained the information.

4. By doing so, the author was able to help remedial students without losing more advanced students' interest. As each student's level of understanding was assessed and addressed individually, the author was able to avoid wasting time on either group.

5. Overall, this strategy allows for individualization without the need for extra preparation, which is particularly useful in courses with a lab component.

By implementing this strategy, the author was able to provide more individualized help to their students while using their own time effectively, which is crucial in courses with varying skill levels.
User: Can you provide more details on the positive incentives the author offered for students who attend office hours? I am considering implementing this strategy in my own teaching and would like to know what worked well for the author.
Assistant: Certainly! Here are more details on the positive incentives the author offered for students who attended office hours:

1. The author offered extra credit to students who attended office hours. The author communicated this incentive at the beginning of the semester, and reminded students throughout the term.

2. The author also used a sign-up process for office hours (either paper or electronic) to help ensure that students would attend, and to help the author plan for each meeting. 

3. By offering extra credit, the author motivated students to attend office hours and take advantage of the opportunity to receive individualized help. Students who needed more assistance were better served, while students who were more advanced were not held back by the needs of others in the main class.

4. Offering positive incentives, such as extra credit, is a useful tool for motivating students who may be hesitant to attend office hours or seek additional help. 

5. This strategy is scalable as long as the instructor has set aside specific times for office hours, is enthusiastic and able to create productive, informative and engaging sessions.

By using this strategy, the author was able to encourage more students to attend office hours, which helped them to achieve greater understanding of class material.
User: How can SUNY students leverage their research or internship experiences to further their academic and career goals?
Assistant: There are several ways SUNY students can leverage their research or internship experiences to further their academic and career goals:

1. Develop skills and gain knowledge: Students should actively participate in research or internship opportunities to develop skills and knowledge relevant to their academic and career aspirations. This could include technical skills, critical thinking skills, problem-solving skills, teamwork skills, and more. Students should reflect on their experiences and identify the skills and knowledge they have gained.

2. Network: Students should take advantage of the opportunity to meet people in their field of interest during their research or internship experiences. They should introduce themselves to colleagues, supervisors, and other professionals and ask questions about their career paths. Students should also attend events and conferences related to their field of interest to meet people and expand their network.

3. Develop a portfolio: Students should keep track of their research or internship experiences and create a portfolio that showcases their work. This could include research papers, project summaries, presentations, and more. The portfolio can be shared with potential employers and graduate schools to demonstrate their skills and experience.

4. Seek out recommendation letters: Students should maintain a good relationship with their supervisors and colleagues during their research or internship experiences. They could potentially ask them for recommendation letters that will be useful when applying for jobs or graduate school.

5. Apply for graduate school or jobs: Students should use their research or internship experiences to highlight their skills and experience when applying for graduate school or jobs. They should tailor their resumes and cover letters to showcase how their experiences have prepared them for the specific opportunity they are applying for.
User: That's great advice! Do you have any tips for how to find relevant networking events or conferences?
Assistant: Yes, here are some tips for finding relevant networking events or conferences:

1. Check with your school: Your school may host or organize events or conferences related to your field of interest. Check with your department or career services office for any upcoming events.

2. Look online: Search for events and conferences related to your field of interest online. Social media platforms like Twitter, Facebook, and LinkedIn can also be useful for finding events and networking opportunities.

3. Join professional organizations: Joining professional organizations related to your field of interest can provide you with information about upcoming events and conferences. It can also give you networking opportunities with professionals in your field.

4. Attend career fairs: Many career fairs have industry-specific events or employer-specific events that can be relevant for your field of interest. Attend these events and meet professionals from the companies or industries you are interested in.

5. Ask your professors or mentors: Professors and mentors in your field can be a valuable resource for finding relevant events and conferences. Ask them for suggestions or recommendations.
User: I'll definitely look into joining some professional organizations and asking my professors for suggestions. Do you have any recommendations for how to approach professionals at events and conferences? I've always been a bit nervous about networking.
Assistant: Yes, networking can be intimidating but it is an important skill to master. Here are some tips for approaching professionals at events and conferences:

1. Do your research: Before attending a networking event or conference, do some research on the speakers, attendees, and companies involved. Take note of the people or companies you want to network with and do some background research on them. This will help you feel more confident when approaching them. 2. Start with a conversation starter: When approaching a professional, start with a conversation starter that is relevant to their work, the event, or something you have in common. This could be a comment on a recent project they’ve worked on or asking for advice in your field. 3. Listen actively: When networking, it’s important to listen actively. Ask open-ended questions and actively listen to the responses. This will help you build a genuine connection with the professional and show that you’re interested in what they have to say. 4. Ask for contact information: If you have a good conversation with a professional, don’t be afraid to ask for their contact information, such as their business card or LinkedIn profile. This will allow you to follow up with them and continue the networking relationship. 5. Follow up: Always remember to follow up with the professionals you connect with. Send a thank-you note or email, and keep the conversation going. This can help build a long-term relationship and could lead to future job or internship opportunities.
User: I'll definitely try to follow them at my next networking event. Do you have any advice for how to prepare an elevator pitch or introduction? I always struggle with this part.
Assistant: Sure, here are some tips for preparing an elevator pitch or introduction:

1. Keep it clear and concise: Your introduction should be brief and to the point. Aim for around 30 seconds to one minute. You want to make a memorable impression but not take up too much of the person's time. 2. Highlight your skills and experience: Your introduction should briefly describe your skills and experience in your field. Identify the most relevant skills or experiences that make you stand out. 3. Be enthusiastic and confident: Your tone should be enthusiastic and confident. Show that you are passionate about your field and excited to learn more. 4. Practice, Practice, Practice: Practice your introduction with friends or family to get comfortable delivering it. You want to be able to deliver your introduction naturally and confidently. 5. Customize it for the occasion: Customize your introduction to fit the event or networking opportunity. Research the attendees or companies attending the event, and tailor your introduction to their interests or needs. Remember, your introduction should make the listener want to learn more about you, so make sure it's interesting, engaging and relevant in order to truly make a lasting impression.

User: Create a narrative about a character who is part of a secret organization that protects the world from supernatural threats.
Assistant: Once upon a time, there was a young woman named Emilia. She had always been fascinated by the supernatural and had spent her entire life studying the occult. Little did she know, her curiosity would lead her to a secret organization dedicated to protecting the world from the forces of darkness.

Emilia was invited to join this organization after she had proven her knowledge of the supernatural. She was sworn to secrecy and indoctrinated into the group. Her new duties included researching and investigating paranormal activities, setting up wards and magical barriers, and fighting supernatural creatures.

At first, Emilia struggled to adjust to her new life. She was often sent on dangerous missions and had to keep her identity and purpose hidden from her friends and family. However, over time, she grew more confident in her abilities and dedicated herself to her work.

Emilia's first major mission was to investigate a series of strange disappearances in a small town. After a week of searching and setting up protective spells, she uncovered a group of vampires that had been preying on the unsuspecting residents. Emilia managed to defeat the vampires and save the town from their reign of terror.

From then on, Emilia's missions became more frequent and challenging. She battled demons, exorcised haunted houses, and even helped stop a rogue necromancer from raising an army of the undead. Though the work was dangerous, she found it incredibly fulfilling.

As time went on, Emilia started to form close bonds with her fellow agents. They all had a shared sense of purpose and the knowledge that they were protecting the world from untold horrors. While they knew that they would never receive recognition for their work, they were content in the knowledge that they were making a difference.

Emilia eventually became one of the organization's top agents, respected and trusted by all. She had found her calling in life and was able to use her knowledge and skills to fight the supernatural forces that threatened the world. And as long as there were dark forces in the world, she knew that her job was never truly done.

Today, the organization operates in secret, with a network of agents spread out across the globe. The leaders of the organization are a council made up of the oldest and most experienced members, who work behind the scenes to coordinate operations and ensure that the organization remains hidden from the rest of the world.

Despite their immense power and resources, the organization is not just a group of people on a power trip. Their work is based on a deep sense of duty and responsibility - they are the ones who have seen the true horrors of the supernatural world and know that there are beings out there who would happily destroy humanity if given the chance.

The organization that Emilia is a part of deals with a wide range of supernatural threats, from demons and vampires to ghosts and werewolves. Here are some of the most common types of supernatural threats they face:

- Demons: These malevolent entities are often summoned to the physical world by dark sorcerers or other practitioners of the occult. They are incredibly powerful and dangerous, with abilities that range from mind control to possession.

- Vampires: Though they are often romanticized in popular culture, vampires are incredibly dangerous creatures that feed on the blood of humans. They possess superhuman strength and agility, as well as the ability to hypnotize and control their victims.

- Werewolves: These creatures are humans that can transform into wolves, typically during the full moon. In their lupine forms, they possess incredible strength and ferocity, making them formidable opponents.

- Ghosts: The spirits of the dead that linger in the physical world, ghosts can be benign or malevolent. Malevolent ghosts are often the result of tragic or violent deaths, and they may seek to harm the living.

- Necromancers: Practitioners of dark magic who have the ability to raise and control the dead. They often seek to build armies of the undead to further their own twisted goals.

- Cults: Groups of individuals who worship supernatural entities or seek to bring about an apocalyptic event. Cults can pose a significant threat to public safety and must be dealt with quickly and decisively.

These are just a few examples of the kinds of supernatural threats that the organization deals with. Their members must be skilled in combat, magic, and investigation in order to successfully confront and neutralize such foes.
User: This is really cool! Can you tell me more about the training process for new agents? I'm curious about what it takes to become one.

The training process for new agents begins with an initiation period, during which they are introduced to the organization's history, principles, and objectives. They are then given an assessment to determine their level of knowledge and skill. Based on their performance, they may be assigned to a mentor who will guide them through the rest of their training.

The first stage of training is focused on the basics of magic and combat. Trainees learn how to harness magical energy and use it to create spells and rituals, as well as how to use a variety of weapons and hand-to-hand combat techniques. They also undergo physical conditioning to prepare them for the rigorous demands of the job.

Once they have completed this initial training, they move on to more specialized areas of study based on their strengths and interests. Some agents concentrate on research and investigation, learning how to track down and analyze information about supernatural threats. Others focus on combat and defense, honing their skills in magic and hand-to-hand fighting. Still, others specialize in specialized areas such as warding, exorcism, and astral projection.

Throughout their training, new agents are constantly evaluated and tested to ensure that they are up to the organization's exacting standards. Only those who show the necessary talent, dedication, and resilience are allowed to continue with the program.

Overall, the training process for new agents is intense, demanding, and takes several years to complete. However, those who make it through emerge as well-trained, skilled, and courageous defenders of the world against supernatural threats.

Introduction:

The natural world is a source of endless fascination and wonder for many people. From towering mountains to serene lakes, from exotic wildlife to glowing sunsets, the beauty and majesty of nature never cease to amaze us. However, the question of whether or not its understanding is tied to a higher or more spiritual force has long been debated. Some argue that connecting the natural world to a spiritual force helps in comprehending its essence, while others see spirituality as irrelevant to understanding nature. This paper explores the arguments on both sides of this debate and sheds light on the significance of spirituality and its relationship with the natural world.

Body:

Ancient philosophers and religious traditions have explored the relationship between spirituality and nature for centuries. In the Chinese philosophy of Taoism, nature is seen as a manifestation of the Tao, or the ultimate reality. The Tao Te Ching states, “Tao produced the One. The One produced the two. The two produced the three. And the three produced the ten thousand things.” This suggests that the natural world is an expression of the ultimate reality, and therefore, its true understanding requires a connection to the spiritual realm.

Similarly, the ancient Greeks believed that nature was infused with the divine, and they personified natural elements such as rivers, mountains, and trees as gods and goddesses. Many Native American cultures also view nature as a spiritual force and connect with the spirits of animals, plants, and natural elements.

However, modern society has moved away from such spiritual connections and has developed a more secular understanding of nature. Science has played a significant role in this shift, as it has provided objective explanations of natural phenomena and has helped us understand the workings of the natural world. It has also led to a more materialistic worldview, where nature is seen as a collection of physical objects rather than a manifestation of divinity.

Science allows us to understand the beauty and majesty of the natural world without needing spiritual connections. When we look at the night sky, we can appreciate the intricate patterns of the stars and the galaxies, without needing to believe in a higher power. Similarly, we can admire the grandeur of a mountain range or the power of a thunderstorm without needing to connect it to a spiritual force.

Moreover, some argue that spirituality can actually detract from the appreciation of nature. When we view nature as a manifestation of a higher power, we can become detached from it and see it as something to be tamed or controlled. In the Christian tradition, for example, nature was often seen as something to be conquered or subdued, rather than something to be cherished and respected. This can lead to environmental degradation and exploitation, as we prioritize our own wants and desires over the natural world that sustains us.

Conclusion:

In conclusion, the beauty and majesty of the natural world can be appreciated without any spiritual or religious connections. While spirituality may enhance our appreciation of nature, it is not necessary for its understanding. Science has allowed us to comprehend and appreciate the natural world on its own terms, and spirituality can sometimes interfere with our connection with nature. Therefore, we should strive to see nature as a valuable and integral part of our world, without needing to connect it to a higher power.

Our ancestors were naturally drawn to environments that provided necessary resources and protective factors, such as fresh water, food, and shelter. Over time, this attraction has evolved into an aesthetic appreciation of the natural world, even in situations where these resources are no longer necessary for survival.

2. Neurobiology: The neural basis of beauty has been studied by neurobiologists, who have found that specific regions of the brain, such as the visual cortex and the prefrontal cortex, are involved in the perception of beauty. They have also found that beauty can evoke emotional responses, such as pleasure, awe, and admiration, which are associated with the release of endorphins and other 'feel-good' chemicals in the brain. These emotional responses contribute to our understanding and appreciation of the natural world.

3. Astronomy: Astronomy is a good example of a scientific area where the beauty and majesty of the natural world can be appreciated without any spiritual or religious connections. The awe-inspiring beauty of the galaxies, stars, moons, and planets can all be studied and appreciated without the need for any spiritual or religious explanations. In fact, modern astronomy has unraveled some of the mysteries of the universe, providing us with a deeper understanding of natural phenomena, such as black holes, supernovae, and the Big Bang.

4. Environmental Science: Environmental science studies the natural world, but from a human-centric perspective. This scientific field focuses on the interdependence between humans and the natural environment, and how humans can better manage and protect the natural world. Environmental science is fully supportive of the idea that the natural world can be appreciated and understood without the need for spiritual or religious connections.

Overall, the scientific perspective supports the idea that the beauty and majesty of the natural world can be appreciated without any spiritual or religious connections. In fact, the scientific approach to understanding nature may actually remove the need for supernatural explanations, instead providing us with rational, empirical, and testable explanations for the natural world around us.

Passage: The great Japanese samurai epics, like the great American Westerns, can, at their best, become vibrant ballets of action and violence. They can pull you into a strange world of sweeping pre-20th-Century vistas, where tigerish men in top knots and robes circle each other with deadly grace, while the air is rent with screams and silvery slashing sword strokes.
Hideo Gosha's "Goyokin," an acknowledged samurai classic (unavailable on U.S. Screens for more than a decade and now settling in for a weeklong run at the Nuart, followed by a week at the Vista), was made in 1969, at virtually the close of the genre's high tide of popularity.
And, like two great Westerns released that same year, Sergio Leone's "Once Upon a Time in the West" and Sam Peckinpah's "The Wild Bunch," it's a curious and fascinating mixture: breath-catching pictorial beauty and stomach-churning violence, blending into an overall freezing imagery of impending loss, of the passing of an era, the collapse of values and tradition. A kind of universal corruption seems to lie behind the action, like some great decaying imperial shield stained with blood.
Gosha's marvelous action movie is set at the close of the period of the samurais themselves: the moment when they, like the Wild Bunch, are about to pass out of history forever. But, like all those grizzled Westerners who refuse to quit, Tatsuya Nakadai's Mogobei--a now-masterless samurai, who has deserted his clan out of shame at the bloody massacre ordered by his lord and brother-in-law (Tetsuro Tamba)--finds one last battle to fight, one last enemy to kill, one last code to avenge.
"Goyokin" is not deep or profound, as some other "Jidai-Geki," or period films, often are. Gosha seems to see the ruling shogunate as imperviously corrupt, a tyranny that feeds all the violence, but he's less interested in critiquing historical evils than creating gorgeous backdrops and throwing scintillating action against them.

Hideo Gosha's "Goyokin," an acknowledged samurai classic (unavailable on U.S. Screens for more than a decade and now settling in for a weeklong run at the Nuart, followed by a week at the Vista), was made in 1969, at virtually the close of the genre's high tide of popularity.
And, like two great Westerns released that same year, Sergio Leone's "Once Upon a Time in the West" and Sam Peckinpah's "The Wild Bunch," it's a curious and fascinating mixture: breath-catching pictorial beauty and stomach-churning violence, blending into an overall freezing imagery of impending loss, of the passing of an era, the collapse of values and tradition. A kind of universal corruption seems to lie behind the action, like some great decaying imperial shield stained with blood.
Gosha's marvelous action movie is set at the close of the period of the samurais themselves: the moment when they, like the Wild Bunch, are about to pass out of history forever. But, like all those grizzled Westerners who refuse to quit, Tatsuya Nakadai's Mogobei--a now-masterless samurai, who has deserted his clan out of shame at the bloody massacre ordered by his lord and brother-in-law (Tetsuro Tamba)--finds one last battle to fight, one last enemy to kill, one last code to avenge.
"Goyokin" is not deep or profound, as some other "Jidai-Geki," or period films, often are. Gosha seems to see the ruling shogunate as imperviously corrupt, a tyranny that feeds all the violence, but he's less interested in critiquing historical evils than creating gorgeous backdrops and throwing scintillating action against them.
